vignette: John, a 76-year-old widowed European-American man who worked as a cashier, had experienced significant trauma during his time in a war zone. The images and sounds of that conflict still haunted him daily, causing profound distress. The traumatic event itself was seared into John’s memory: the constant sound of gunfire, the explosions shaking the ground beneath him, and the sight of destruction all around him. These vivid memories were mostly visual, and when they surfaced, he felt as if he were reliving the experience all over again. The emotions that accompanied these memories had left him feeling completely numb, as though he was watching someone else’s life play out. John’s negative appraisals significantly influenced how he processed his memories. He believed that the world was an inherently dangerous place, a conviction that made it difficult for him to find any solace in positive experiences. The idea that he was no longer capable of doing what once defined him—working steadily and supporting others—also added to his distress. John’s loss of faith in people, life, and higher power further reinforced the belief that he could not trust anyone or anything anymore. These negative appraisals intensified the emotional impact of his memories. Whenever John recalled the frightening events, they felt as if they were happening all over again, heightening his sense of vulnerability and danger. This cycle led him to seek meaning in why such a traumatic event had happened to him, but he found no answers that provided comfort. To cope with these overwhelming emotions and memories, John developed several maladaptive strategies. He avoided driving or being a passenger in a vehicle because the sound and movement reminded him of explosions and gunfire. When positive feelings surfaced, he pushed them away; they felt unsafe given his heightened sense of danger. This avoidance only served to reinforce his negative appraisals and made it harder for him to engage with the world around him. John’s hypervigilance was another significant issue. He was superalert and watchful at all times, constantly on guard against potential threats. At work as a cashier, he found himself watching other customers closely for any signs that they might harm him. This constant state of alertness made it difficult for him to fall asleep because he felt he needed to stay awake in order to be prepared. The cycle was tightening around John. His hypervigilance and threat monitoring led to increased avoidance behaviors, which in turn reinforced his negative appraisals. Each time he relived the traumatic event, he felt more certain that the world was dangerous and that he could no longer trust others or himself. This left him feeling isolated and unable to engage with life. John’s maladaptive strategies also influenced how he processed his memories and negative appraisals. His avoidance of positive feelings made it harder for him to find any sense of safety or meaning, reinforcing the belief that the world was inherently dangerous and unpredictable. The consequence of this cycle was a significant impact on his work and daily life; his hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors began to affect his ability to interact with customers and perform his job effectively. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function normally, both in his occupation and personal life. He was most afraid of being trapped in a cycle of fear and distrust, unable to connect with others or find any sense of peace. Despite his fears, he hoped that therapy might provide some relief from these overwhelming memories and negative beliefs about the world around him.
